Program Name:  Micah.java 
Input File:  micah.dat 
 
Micah wants to analyze the instructions for his team’s automated robot and make sure the robot visits the expected waypoints on 
the field.  The field of play is labeled as a two-dimensional grid.   The robot always starts at the origin position, (0,0), the 
center of the field. The instructions are listed with a direction (N, S, E, W) followed by a (positive) number of steps for the 
robot to take in that direction.  N is in the positive y direction, S is in the negative y direction, E is in the positive x direction, and 
W is in the negative x direction.  The field is a grid with x values in the range [-25, 25] and y values in the range [-25,25].  There 
is a wall which will keep the robot from going off the field.  If a robot runs into a wall, it just stops the current leg at the edge 
and goes on to the next leg. 
 
Input:  The first line contains an integer, T, which is the number of test cases (1 <= T <= 10).  The next T groups of lines will 
begin with a single integer, N (1 <= N <= 25), representing the number of legs of the robot’s journey.  The following N lines 
will consist of a direction, D (N, S, E, W), and an integer, S (0 <= S <= 25), for the number of steps for the robot to take in 
the given direction. 
 
Output:  Each test case’s output will begin and end with 25 #’s.  Next, the output should report, on separate lines, each leg of 
the robot’s journey with the coordinates of the ending location with an arrow (->) in between. Print a blank line after all the legs 
are displayed.  The next line will be “Final location”, a single space, and “: (x,y)” with x,y being the coordinates at 
the end of the robot’s completed run.  The next line will be “Distance”, seven (7) spaces, and “: d” with d being the total

“Commands”, seven (7) spaces, and ”: N=n S=s E=e W=w” where n, s, e, and w are the number of legs taken in each 
direction.  Add a blank line after the closing line of #s.

5.  Bish 
 
Program Name:  Bish.java 
Input File:  bish.dat 
 
During a recent field trip, you got separated from your classmates and trapped on a volcanic island. Luckily there is a shop 
nearby that will sell you boots to traverse the molten island and rejoin your friends, however you’re not sure if you have enough 
money to purchase the correct boots. Each pair of boots can withstand temperatures up to K – and if you step on a piece of 
molten rock hotter than K then you will burn and perish. There’s a handy map of the island represented by an 𝑁× 𝑀grid on the 
wall of the shop where each grid space is the temperature of that spot on the island, so you decide to use your laptop and write a 
program to calculate the minimum value K required to get off the island. 
 
Input:   
The input line will contain a single integer 𝑁(1 ≤𝑁≤100) denoting the number of volcanoes to escape. The next 𝑁 input lines 
will start with two integers 𝑅, 𝐶 (1 ≤𝑅, 𝐶≤1000) representing the number of rows and columns in the grid representation of 
the island. The following 𝑅 lines will contain 𝐶 integers 𝑇𝑖,𝑗 (0 ≤𝑇𝑖,𝑗≤109) denoting the temperature of that cell. The next line 
will contain four space separated integers 𝑋1, 𝑌1, 𝑋2, 𝑌2 representing the starting position and the desired ending position. 
 
Output:   
For each volcanic island, print the smallest value 𝐾 required to escape the island. 
 
Sample input: 
3 
3 3 
1 3 2 
6 5 4 
9 8 1 
0 0 2 2 
2 2 
1 10 
2 3 
0 0 1 1 
5 5 
42 42 42 42 42 
42 42 42 42 42 
42 42 42 42 42 
42 42 42 42 42 
42 42 42 42 42 
0 0 4 4 
 
Sample output: 
4 
3 
42

6. Jackie 
 
 
Program Name:  Jackie.java 
Input File:  jackie.dat 
 
Jackie has joined the chess club. She is new to the game, and wants you to write a program to help her determine possible 
combinations of moves, given the pieces already on the board. You will be given all the pieces, and their positions, on an 8x8 
board (1-indexed), and you need to determine how many valid combinations of moves exist for all the pieces on the board, 
without the pieces interfering with each other’s moves. To determine move combinations, first determine all the possible moves 
each piece can make from their current position, given the knowledge that rooks can move right, left, up, or down up to 7 spaces, 
bishops can move up to 7 spaces on any of the diagonals, and a queen can do either. Each move combination is made up of 1 
valid move (and finishing position on the board) per each piece, note that a valid move for a piece is to stay in its current 
position. Once a combo has been chosen, you will need to validate that the combo has no collisions. Collisions occur, when on 
the course of making your move, two or more of the pieces move into the same space at the same time. For each combo, assume 
you will be making all moves simultaneously, moving each piece one space at a time until all pieces are in the positions you 
chose when you made the combo. If two pieces move into the same space at the same time, then that causes a collision, and the 
move combo is no longer valid. Pieces can swap places while on their paths to the finishing positions, without causing a 
collision. See the example section for an explanation of some of the possible scenarios. 
 
Example: All positions are in form row,column 
We have a rook in position 3,3, and a queen in position 2, 2, as shown in the sample board below. We can choose any of the 
valid moves for those two pieces (rooks can go up, down, left, right, queen can do the same and also diagonals). For example, if 
we choose queen to 6,2 and rook to 3,6, there are no collisions, and this would make a valid move combination. If we choose to 
not move the rook, and move the queen to any point along the down-right diagonal, the queen cannot move as the rook will 
always be in the way, so none of those move combos would be valid. However, if we move the rook to 2,3, we can move the 
queen along the diagonal, because the rook will move off of the diagonal at the same time as we move the queen along the 
diagonal (shown in the second example, we did rook to 2,3 and queen to 5,5). Now, let’s explain the first sample board below. 
We chose as our move combo, queen to 2,8 and rook to 1,3. So we try the move combo, moving the pieces one space at a time 
simultaneously until they both get to the finishing position, or there is a collision, signified by the X (which there is in this case at 
space 2,3 on the first space moved for both pieces)

.Q......    ..X..... | .Q......    ..R.....    ..R.....    ..R..... 
..R.....    ........ | ..R.....    ..Q.....    ........    ........ 
........    ........ | ........    ........    ...Q....    ........ 
........ -> ........ | ........ -> ........ -> ........ -> ....Q... 
........    ........ | ........    ........    ........    ........ 
........    ........ | ........    ........    ........    ........ 
........    ........ | ........    ........    ........    ........

The input will begin with one integer, n (0 < n <= 100). Each test case will begin with a line with an integer p (0 < p <= 
10), denoting the number of pieces present on the 8x8 board. The following line will contain p space-separated strings (“rook”, 
“bishop”, or “queen”), denoting the type of each of the p pieces in order. The line after than will contain p integers, each 
denoting the row coordinate of the position of that piece, with the following line containing another p integers, denoting the 
column coordinate of the position of that piece. 
 
Output:   
For each test case, output the number of combinations of valid moves of all pieces on the board, excluding the options which 
have any collisions, following the methodology outlined in the example section.

2

queen

1 5 
 
Sample output:  
22 
206

7.  Bash 
 
Program Name:  Bash.java 
Input File:  bash.dat 
 
Bored during class, you go over to your friends Maelle and Alicia to see if they want to play some games and find that they’re 
busy doing some smart stuff you can’t be bothered to understand. Left alone, you decide to write a simple program to play with 
you to have some fun. The game of choice is Ultimate Tic Tac Toe, which is like a normal game of tic tac toe but within each 
square is a new tic tac toe board! When a player makes a move inside a square, the next player must move in the large square 
corresponding to the small square that was played. For example, in the board below if a player makes a move in square 3 then 
the next move must be made in the top right corner of the larger board. 
 
The first move always takes place on the middle board. If a move takes you to an already finished board (the board is full or has 
a winner) then you will choose to move on the first available board 1-9 where 1 is top left and 9 is bottom right. Both you and 
the robot make random moves each turn, since you can’t be bothered to try and play optimally. When generating a move, 
number the squares 1-9 like above skipping filled in spaces, then generate a random number 1-N where N is the highest value on 
that board using random.nextInt(a,b). The robot will always move first placing Xs and you will go second playing Os. Winning a 
sub-game follows normal tic tac toe rules, where the first player to make 3 in a row horizontally, vertically, or diagonally wins. 
The winner of the ultimate tic tac toe game is the player to win 3 sub-games horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. 
 
Input:   
The input file will contain two values, an integer 𝑁(1 ≤𝑁≤106) denoting the number of games to be played and a long value 
𝐿 representing a random seed. The random seed provided will be used to generate a new random seed for each of the 𝑁 games 
using random.nextLong(). 
 
Output:   
For each game output the winner “X wins!”, “O wins!”, or “Tie” and the final board state like shown below. After all games 
output the statistics for X, O, and Tied games to two decimal places. 
 
Sample input: 
3 235325225275745653

8. Steve 
 
 
Program Name:  Steve.java  
Input File:  steve.dat 
 
Steve is trapped in a maze with his friends! He needs your help to write a program to find out how long it will take them all to 
escape as efficiently as possible. They have been given a flashlight and an aerial view map of the maze, denoting by the 
following characters: 
 
S – Denotes the starting point in the maze (where Steve and all of his friends begin) 
 
E – Denotes the end point of the maze, where all people need to end up. 
 
# - Denotes a wall in the maze, cannot be passed. 
 
. – Denotes an empty space in the maze, can be passed. 
 
You may only move up, down, left, and right, and you can assume all sections (characters) are equal in size. 
You will also be given the speeds of all the people in the maze, i.e. how long it will take to pass one section of the maze (one 
character). In order to escape the maze, all people must get from the start to the end, but they can only do that if they have the 
map and the flashlight, it is too dark and confusing otherwise. The maze is only wide enough for a maximum 2 people to travel 
at a time, so the process is: two people take the map and flashlight to the end, one comes back with the flashlight and map and 
either keeps the map/flashlight or gives it to someone else, and then two people travel to the end again, with one coming back, 
until all people have made it to the end. Keep in mind, when 2 people travel, they can only move as fast as the slower of the two 
of them. 
 
Input:   
The input will begin with one integer, n (0 < n <= 1000) denoting the number of test cases to follow. Each test case will 
begin with a line with three space-separated integers r (0 < r <= 10), c (0 < c <= 10), and p (0 < p <= 10), 
denoting the number of rows and columns in the map given, and the number of people (including Steve) who need to escape the 
maze, respectively. The following r lines will each contain c characters denoting the aerial view of the maze. The following line 
will contain p space separated integers denoting the speeds of each of the people in the maze.  
 
Output:   
For each test case, output the minimum amount of time required for all of the people in the maze to get out. If the maze is not 
solvable for any reason (too many walls, no end point), output the string “Phooey”. 
 
Sample input:   
2 
4 5 4 
S..#. 
#..#. 
##... 
#.E.# 
1 2 5 8 
3 6 3 
S..#.E 
##..#. 
..#... 
2 4 6 
 
Sample output:  
75 
108

11.  Verso 
 
Program Name:  Verso.java 
Input File:  verso.dat 
 
Verso is a linguistics professor who has become obsessed with palindromes – words that read the same forwards and backwards. 
While grading papers, Verso noticed that any string can be broken into palindromic segments, but different ways of breaking 
them up require different amounts of "mental effort" to verify. 
 
Verso has developed a cost model for splitting strings: each split at position 𝑖 (creating a boundary between characters at index 𝑖 
and 𝑖+ 1) costs exactly 𝑖 points of mental effort. For example, splitting "RACE" into "R", "A", "CE" requires a split after 
position 1 (cost 1) and after position 2 (cost 2), for a total cost of 3. However, if each resulting segment isn't a palindrome, Verso 
gets frustrated and the solution is invalid, as would be the case with the split provided above. 
 
Verso wants to break strings into palindromic segments while minimizing his total mental effort. Note that every single character 
is considered a palindrome on its own, so a valid solution always exists. 
 
Input:   
The first line will consist of a single integer 𝑇, 1 ≤𝑇≤100, denoting the number of test cases to follow. Each of the following 
𝑇 lines will consist of a single string 𝑆 consisting of uppercase English letters only, where  
1 ≤|𝑆| ≤103.  
 
Output:   
For each test case, on its own line, print the minimum total cost to partition the string into palindromic segments. If the entire 
string is already a palindrome, the answer is 0 (no splits needed). 
 
Sample input:  
6 
A 
AB 
ABA 
RACECAR 
ABC 
ABCD 
Sample output:  
0 
1 
0 
0 
3 
6 
 
Explanation: 
The first, third, and fourth test cases are all already palindromes, and thus their cost is 0. 
 
The second requires a split in between “A” and “B” which costs 1. This is the minimum (and only) way to split the string, and 
this its minimum cost is 1. 
 
The fifth string requires a split in between “A”, “B”, and “C”, which costs 3 in total (1 for A|BC and 2 for B|C).  
 
The sixth string works exactly the same as the fifth but additionally requires a split between C|D which costs 3, brining the total 
to 6.

Program Name:  Maelle.java 
Input File:  maelle.dat 
 
Maelle is good friends with Alicia who, earlier this year, was learning about the formal definitions of Graphs and Trees. 
Previously, Alicia had mentioned that she had a sage, oracle friend who had determined the connectedness of each graph ahead 
of time; however, as it turns out, Maelle was that friend! As a quick reminder, Alicia learned: 
• 
A graph 𝐺= (𝑉, 𝐸) is formally defined to be composed of a set of vertices 𝑉= {𝑣1,𝑣2,…, 𝑣𝑛} and edges  
𝐸= {𝑒1,𝑒2,… , 𝑒𝑚} where edge 𝑒𝑖= (𝑢, 𝑣), 𝑢,𝑣∈𝑉 indicates that a relationship exists between vertex 𝑢 and vertex 𝑣.  
• 
A graph 𝐺 is said to be “connected” if every pair of vertices 𝑣𝑖, 𝑣𝑗 is connected in 𝐺. A pair of vertices 𝑣𝑖, 𝑣𝑗 is said to be 
connected if there exists some simple path from 𝑣𝑖 to 𝑣𝑗 (denoted 𝑣𝑖⇝𝑣𝑗) via some subset of edges in 𝐸. 
o 
An undirected graph 𝐺 is said to be “disconnected” if it is not connected. 
o 
A directed graph 𝐺 is said to be “weakly connected” if by replacing all directed edges in 𝐸 with undirected ones (call 
this new set 𝐸′), then graph 𝐺′ = (𝑉,𝐸′) is connected. 
o 
A directed graph 𝐺 is said to be “strongly connected” if for every pair of vertices 𝑣𝑖,𝑣𝑗∈𝑉, then both  
𝑣𝑖⇝𝑣𝑗 and 𝑣𝑗⇝𝑣𝑖 hold. That is, a graph is strongly connected if it is a connected directed graph. 
o 
A directed graph 𝐺 is said to be “unilaterally connected” if, for every pair of vertices 𝑣𝑖,𝑣𝑗∈𝑉, then either 𝑣𝑖⇝𝑣𝑗 
and/or 𝑣𝑗⇝𝑣𝑖 hold.  
o 
A directed graph 𝐺 is said to be “disconnected” if it is not weakly, strongly, or unilaterally connected. 
Unfortunately, Maelle has recently lost her sage powers and is unable to automatically classify the connectedness of each graph 
anymore. In order to maintain her reputation, help Maelle in determining the connectedness of Alicia’s graphs.

also assume that both the directedness and cyclicity fields have been filled out with the corresponding
